newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan to discuss delayed oil deal with Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Jordan to discuss delayed oil deal with Iraq.

text.p: Jordan will seek to persuade Baghdad to ease demands for higher prices for Iraqi oil exports to the kingdom in talks with Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz, officials said on Sunday.
Aziz was expected in Amman late on Sunday on his way to Paris and officials said he would meet Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti during the stop-over.
"The talks should close the gap on the annual oil deal that has not been signed yet," one official who requested anonymity told Reuters.

Jordan and Iraq failed at the start of the month to conclude terms for the 1997 trade protocol under which Iraq supplies Jordan with most of its energy needs -- around 75,000 bpd of crude oil and petroleum products -- at concessionary terms.
The Iraqi oil exports to Jordan, worth well over $400 million a year, are exempt from U.N. trade sanctions slapped on Baghdad in 1990 for its invasion of Kuwait.
Jordan pays for only half the oil, and not in cash but by exporting industrial goods to Iraq. The other half goes towards settlement of more than $1 billion of accumulated Iraqi debts.
Iraq wants to cut the share of free oil to 45 percent from 50 percent and reduce the discount offered on the remainder to $2 per barrel below world prices, officials said.
Jordan hopes it will persuade Iraq to accept to keep the price unchanged at $15.25 per barrel -- what it has been paying despite steep rises in oil prices in the second half of 1996.
A meeting of the two countries' joint ministerial committee scheduled for January 6 in Baghdad was postponed because of disagreement over the pricing.
Jordanian officials said they did not believe Iraq's demand was political retaliation for King Hussein's distancing himself from Iraqi President Saddam Hussein since 1995.
"We do not smell any political motives, only improving Iraq's financial returns," another official said.
He said Iraq had agreed to Jordan's request to raise the oil supplies in 1997 by seven percent to meet growth in local consumption.
Jordan has been trying to mend fences with Iraq since the announcement last month of the implementation of an Iraqi oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
Jordanian businessmen say they have won orders in tough competition to supply Iraq with a range of goods worth more than $120 million under the accord.
